## Part 1: Verse-by-verse notes (traditional reading)

**v. 1**
- The Greek word for Saul's "approval" means he enjoyed persecuting Christians, not that he went along reluctantly. This is the first persecution of the whole church; earlier, only the apostles had been targeted. (EW)
- Gill agrees the word means consent "with pleasure and delight." He thinks "all scattered" means the preachers, not every member, because devout men stayed to bury Stephen and Saul still found people to arrest. (Gill)
- Wesley says the same: not the whole church, or no one would have been left for the apostles to teach or for Saul to persecute. It was the teachers who left, while the apostles stayed with the flock even though they were in the most danger. (Wesley)
- Ellicott thinks the persecution fell mainly on Hellenistic believers who taught, like Stephen, that the old customs would pass away. The apostles still worshipped in the Temple, which may have protected them. He says the word "consenting" suggests Saul directed the killing rather than throwing stones himself. (Ellicott)
- PA calls this a turning point: the church now expands beyond Jerusalem. (PA)
- Henry sees Samson's riddle here: the persecution meant to wipe out the church ended up enlarging it. (MHC)

**v. 2**
- Most commentators think the "devout men" were pious Jews, not believers. By openly siding with Stephen they took a real personal risk. (PA)
- Ellicott reads the public mourning as a protest, probably by moderate Pharisees like Gamaliel or Nicodemus. (Ellicott)
- Gill notes that Jewish rules said not to mourn publicly for someone executed by stoning, so these men broke that custom. (Gill)
- Wesley says they feared God more than persecution. (Wesley)

**v. 3**
- Wesley says the Greek pictures a furious wild animal, and that Saul spared no one, men or women. (Wesley)
- Gill links Saul to Benjamin's "ravening wolf" in Genesis 49:27. (Gill)
- Ellicott points to Paul's own later admission of "insane" fury (Acts 26:11). (Ellicott)

**v. 4**
- The scattered believers were mostly "accidental missionaries," ordinary people talking about Jesus, not official preachers. (EW)
- Ellicott quotes the saying that "the blood of martyrs is the seed of the Church." (Ellicott)
- Wesley notes that Luke picks this story up again in Acts 11:19. (Wesley)

**v. 5**
- Jews generally despised Samaritans, yet Philip preached to them. Guzik says Jesus had removed that prejudice from Philip's heart. (EW)
- Henry says the word means Philip *proclaimed* Christ, the way a new king is proclaimed across his lands. The Samaritans were already expecting a Messiah (John 4:25). (MHC)
- Wesley: with Stephen gone, Philip, his fellow deacon and not the apostle, takes his place. (Wesley)

**v. 6**
- The verb tense shows the Samaritans kept on paying attention, again and again. (PA)
- Ellicott thinks the miracles strengthened a faith that was already there; they were not its foundation. (Ellicott)

**v. 7**
- The physical miracles are pictures of spiritual power. The gospel still drives out unclean spirits and strengthens the weak. (Biblical Illustrator: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/acts-8.html)

**v. 8**
- The joy came from real spiritual power, but above all from Christ being preached. (EW)
- Gill sees joy for souls (salvation) and for bodies (healing and deliverance). (Gill)
- Ellicott suggests Luke may have heard this story from Philip himself in Caesarea (Acts 21:8). (Ellicott)

**vv. 9–11**
- Gill: Simon was a magician who may have claimed to be the Messiah the Samaritans expected. (Gill)
- Ellicott: Simon claimed to be some kind of incarnation of divine power. (Ellicott)
- Pulpit: the later stories about Simon are "full of fable." Irenaeus calls him the founder of heresy, and his followers called him "the Power of God." (Pulpit)
- Constable: his magic was real sorcery by demonic power, not sleight of hand. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-8.html)
- Guzik: the Samaritans wrongly assumed that real spiritual power must come from God. (EW)
- Wesley's comment: so witchcraft really did exist once. (Wesley)

**v. 12**
- Guzik, quoting Williams, sees nothing lacking in the Samaritans' faith; otherwise Philip would not have baptized them. (EW)
- Wesley: they "saw and felt the real power of God, and submitted" to it. (Wesley)
- Gill says they were baptized by immersion. (Gill)

**v. 13: Was Simon really converted?**
- Guzik: outward Christian behaviour doesn't prove a real conversion. (EW)
- PA gathers several views:
  - Longenecker: Simon's belief rested on miracles, like the faith in John 2:23–25.
  - A.T. Robertson: he was an unconverted man.
  - Wiersbe: Simon stayed near Philip to watch the miracles, perhaps to learn how they were done.
- Ellicott: he had faith without repentance or love. His baptism brought no new birth (see Part 2). (Ellicott)
- Wesley: "believed" means only that he was convinced the message was true. (Wesley)
- Pulpit: Simon is the first baptized person who went on to disgrace the faith, an example of tares among the wheat. (Pulpit)
- MacLaren: his faith was unreal because it changed nothing. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/acts-8.html)

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: the news showed that Jesus' earlier ban on preaching in Samaria (Matthew 10:5) had ended, as Acts 1:8 foretold. Peter and John were sent to approve the new converts. (Ellicott)
- Gangel, quoted in PA: "Time to bring in the first team!" (PA)

**vv. 15–17**
- Ellicott: the prayer was for a gift like Pentecost. The word "fallen" points to a sudden, unexpected change, with new powers. (Ellicott)
- Wesley: was the gift miraculous powers or sanctifying grace? "Probably in both." (Wesley)
- Gill: "only baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus" says nothing about the baptismal formula. They were surely baptized in the threefold name of Father, Son and Spirit. (Gill)
- PA: Philip's preaching lacked nothing. The delay assured the Samaritans they were full members, fully blessed by the Jerusalem leaders. (PA)
- Tuck (Pulpit homilies): in those days no one received the Spirit without some visible sign of power for service. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-8.html)

**vv. 18–19**
- Ellicott: something visible happened; people spoke in tongues and prophesied. The word "simony" (buying church offices or spiritual power) comes from this incident. (Ellicott)
- Gill agrees that what Simon "saw" must have been outward and visible. (Gill)
- PA: Simon wants the power to give the Spirit, but says nothing about people repenting and being saved. (PA)
- Henry: Simon insulted the apostles by treating them as men who would do anything for money. He was after money like Balaam, and he had never truly been humbled. (MHC)

**v. 20**
- Guzik: we cannot buy God's gifts. He notes J.B. Phillips' blunt rendering of Peter's words. (EW)
- Ellicott: literally, "thy money be together with thee, for perdition." (Ellicott)
- Pulpit: the later church offence called simony is only "a very faint analogy" to what Simon did. (Pulpit)

**v. 21**
- Wesley: "part" means a share bought by purchase; "lot" means a share given freely. Simon had neither. Peter could see Simon's heart, but Wesley says the apostles did not have a general power to read everyone's heart. (Wesley)
- Gill: Simon had no real grace in him; his heart was full of greed, ambition and hypocrisy. (Gill)
- HCSB Study Bible, quoted in PA: this confirms Simon was never truly converted. (PA)

**v. 22**
- Wesley and Henry both read "perhaps" the same way. The doubt was whether Simon would truly repent, not whether God would forgive him if he did. (Wesley; MHC)
- PA: Simon had not committed the unpardonable sin. (PA)
- Guzik: Peter didn't try to cast out a "demon of bitterness." He called Simon to repent and pray. (EW)

**v. 23**
- Pulpit: "gall" is a figure for bitterness (Lamentations 3:15, 19). "Bond of iniquity" echoes Isaiah 58:6. (Pulpit)
- Wesley reads the phrase as the highest degree of wickedness, which brings misery to the soul. (Wesley)
- Trapp: sin is a deadly poison, best got rid of quickly by confession. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/acts-8.html)

**v. 24**
- Guzik: Simon felt real conviction but asked to escape the consequences rather than humble himself. Church tradition says he became a dangerous false teacher, though he may have repented. (EW)
- PA: there is no sign of true repentance. (PA)
- Gill: "ye have spoken" suggests John agreed with Peter's words. (Gill)

**v. 25**
- Pulpit homiletics: the apostles went home grateful even though Simon's fall had hurt them. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/acts/8.htm)

**v. 26**
- Gill: guessing which angel this was is "too curious"; it was one of God's ministering spirits. (Gill)
- Wesley: there were two roads to Gaza, one through desert and one through populated country. (Wesley)
- Ellicott: better translated "an angel." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/8-26.htm)
- Barclay: there was an Old Gaza (destroyed in 93 BC) and a New Gaza, which explains the "desert" description. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/8-37.html)
- Guzik: Philip left a fruitful ministry to obey God. "God's workmen change, but God's work goes on." (https://enduringword.com/leaving-a-successful-season/)

**v. 27**
- Wesley: senior officials were often called eunuchs even when they literally weren't. "Candace" was the title for all Ethiopia's queens. (Wesley)
- Gill: Candace ruled the Ethiopians of Meroë. Gill also takes "eunuch" as a title of office here. He reports a tradition that the eunuch later preached in other lands. (Gill)
- Henry: he was a eunuch "not in body, but in office," and this Ethiopia was in Africa. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/8-37.html)
- A Bible Hub Q&A cites Irenaeus' report that the eunuch went home and preached in Ethiopia. (https://biblehub.com/q/Ethiopian_eunuch_in_Acts_8_27_Significance.htm)

**v. 28**
- Wesley: "God meeteth those that remember him in his ways." Use travel time well. (Wesley)
- Henry: people of high standing should set an example of devotion. (MHC)

**v. 29**
- Gill: here it is the Holy Spirit speaking, not the angel. (Gill)
- Guzik: Philip was led by the Spirit, not by his own whims. (EW)

**v. 30**
- Wesley: Philip went straight to the point, without small talk about the weather or news. (Wesley)
- Gill: Philip asked about the meaning, not the language. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/8-30.html)
- PA: the chariot may have been a slow ox-cart. (PA)

**v. 31**
- Wesley sees modesty and a hunger to learn. (Wesley)
- Guzik: reading the Bible helps little without understanding, and God sent Philip to give it. (EW)

**vv. 32–33**
- Wesley: many people have been converted by reading Isaiah 53. "His generation" means his countless spiritual offspring (Isaiah 53:10). (Wesley)
- Henry instead reads "generation" as Christ's endless life in heaven. (MHC)

**v. 34**
- Guzik lists the old answers to the eunuch's question: the servant is Israel, or Isaiah himself, or the Messiah. (EW)

**v. 35**
- NET: the conversation probably drew on other scriptures already quoted in Acts. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=act+8:35-37)

**v. 36**
- Wesley thinks the eunuch had probably been circumcised; otherwise Cornelius would not count as the first Gentile convert. (Wesley)
- NET: the question means, "I should get baptized, right?" (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=act+8:35-37)

**v. 37** (textual details are in Part 2)
- Henry: the confession is short but covers what matters. (MHC)
- Gill: the faith required is sincere, not necessarily strong. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/8-37.html)

**v. 38**
- NET: Philip, who was not one of the Twelve, performs the baptism. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Act+8:37-40&mode=print&theme=wiki)

**v. 39**
- Wesley: Philip was carried away with miraculous speed, as happened to several prophets. (Wesley)
- Guzik: Philip was supernaturally moved. The eunuch's joy after Philip vanished shows his faith rested on God, not on Philip. (https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/a-miracle-of-transportation/)
- NET: the response to the gospel is rejoicing. (NET link under v. 38)
- Constable: the contrast between Simon and the Ethiopian is like the contrast between Gehazi and Naaman. (Constable link under vv. 9–11)

**v. 40**
- NET: Azotus is the Old Testament Ashdod. This Caesarea is the coastal city, not Caesarea Philippi. (NET link under v. 38)
- Ellicott: Philip later settled in Caesarea (Acts 21:8). (Ellicott)
- Guzik: Philip didn't wait for another miracle; he got back to evangelism. (EW devotional link under v. 39)

## Part 2: Where traditions differ

I couldn't search Pentecostal (ag.org, samstorms), Reformed (gty, desiringgod, ligonier) or Lutheran (lcms, 1517) sites. What follows comes from older commentators who belong to those traditions, or from views reported by others.

**vv. 14–17: Why the Spirit came after baptism**
- Guzik sets out three views (EW):
  1. The Samaritans weren't truly converted until Peter and John came.
  2. They were converted, and then received the Spirit in a later experience that is a pattern for believers today.
  3. They were converted, but God held back the Spirit this once to keep the Jerusalem and Samaritan churches united.
- View 2 is the classic Pentecostal position, but I couldn't read that tradition's own sites.
- PA takes the one-off, unity view. (PA)
- Gill says the gifts were outward and visible, not the inward grace of salvation. (Gill)
- Wesley leaves it open: probably both gifts and grace. (Wesley)

**v. 13: Simon's faith and baptism**
- Calvinist and evangelical reading: Simon was never "once saved." True salvation shows itself by persevering, and a profession without repentance is invalid (New Geneva Study Bible). (PA)
- Ellicott (Anglican) takes a sacramental view. Simon's baptism brought no new birth, but if he later repented, its grace would become real without a second baptism; Peter does not tell him to be baptized again. (Ellicott)
- Biblical Illustrator: Simon shows there is a visible church as well as an invisible one, since he was baptized and accepted by apostles. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/8-13.html)

**v. 38: How baptism was done**
- Gill (Baptist) says the Samaritans were baptized by immersion (his note on v. 12). (Gill)
- Wesley: "went down into the water" means getting down from the chariot. It does not follow that this was immersion, and the text says nothing either way. (Wesley)

**v. 37: The added verse**
- NET: only a few later manuscripts have it. It is "clearly not a part of the original text," but it shows how early Christians viewed a confession of faith. (https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Act&chapter=8&verse=37)
- Gill argues, following Beza, that it should not be removed because it records a genuine apostolic confession. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/8-37.html)
- Light of Israel commentary: probably a well-meaning copyist added it because he assumed there could be no baptism without a confession. (same page)

**v. 14 and vv. 18–20: Protestant comments aimed at Rome**
- Wesley: the apostles *sent* Peter, so the apostles as a group were at least his equal. (Wesley)
- Henry calls the sale of pardons and indulgences in the Roman church the same sin as Simon's. (MHC)
- Gill says simony became widespread in Rome, so popes are more Simon Magus's successors than Simon Peter's. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/8-18.htm)

## Part 3: Other views

**Catholic (v. 37)**
- Catholic Answers: the verse is left out of modern Bibles because the oldest manuscripts lack it, not to hide anything; the Douay-Rheims includes it. Quoting the Navarre Bible, it calls the verse a very old addition shaped by the baptismal service.
- The same article uses the verse to teach that adults need faith before baptism, while infants are baptized "in the faith of the Church."
- https://www.catholic.com/qa/why-is-acts-837-omitted-from-many-bible-translations
- I couldn't reach any Catholic or Orthodox reading of vv. 14–17 (confirmation or chrismation).

**Modern scholarship (vv. 27–39)**
- Bible Odyssey: the eunuch was "probably a high official" of "the Candace," meaning the queen mother. (https://web-japan.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/ethiopia/)
- Disability reading: the story shows that bodies of every kind were welcome in the early church. The servant's humiliation and lack of descendants in v. 33 may have matched the eunuch's own situation. (https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-ethiopian-eunuch-from-a-disability-perspective/)
- Queer reading: his identity, both religious and gendered, is left unclear. His question "What is to prevent me?" asks how far baptism reaches, and the rest of Acts works through the answer. (https://web-japan.bibleodyssey.org/articles/ethiopian-eunuch-from-a-queer-perspective/)
- Bible.org: his race and possible physical condition would have kept him from approaching God, but God came looking for him. (https://bible.org/seriespage/13-ethiopian-eunuch-acts-826-40)

**Not found**
- Pentecostal, Reformed and Lutheran teachers' own sites.
- Catholic and Orthodox views on vv. 14–17.
- Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, for example of v. 20.
